questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: New location to explore, closeness to nature, the outdoors

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: the language spoken in the country of exchange, proximity to nature and outdoor activities

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The exchange office at the University of Victoria was easily located on campus and the staff was incredibly kind and helpful. The only hard aspect was that the time change to the office in Denmark made it a little hard to communicate efficiently, but all was solved in the end.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Upon arrival (in late august) I had not been enrolled in the classes that I needed yet, and the exchange office helped me understand the enrollment online system, find classes that I could enroll in, contact professors that had initially denied my application to be in their class, and helped me understand the way the class syllabus worked at UVIC

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Orientation week at UVIC was helpful both academically and socially.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I was lucky, because I had a personal contact in Victoria that knew of an available room in a student house off-campus. I have heard from other exchange students, that it is very hard to find off-campus housing, since the university is not assisting in this matter. Most students I knew of had found their off-campus housing through Facebook-Groups (and the most effective way was to post a short post (with pictures of yourself) to the group and say a bit about who you are and what you are looking for).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Off-campus living is most definitely a good idea, especially because those that live ON-campus are mostly first-year students (and in Canada they are 17-18 year olds), which means that those that are closer to Danish uni students in age all live off-campus. I would say that most off-campus living situations are a house or an apartment shared by 3-6 students. There are some exchange students that didn't find housing until they arrived, so for the first weeks they stayed in an AirBnB or a hostel downtown (and some exchange students even ended up renting an AirBnB for longterm). I recommend trying to stay in areas that are close to the campus (Gordon Head, Arbutus, Cadboro Bay, Uplands - especially if you can get access to a bike). Downtown and Fernwood are also very nice options, but a bit further to campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was lucky, but speaking for most students it seems like it is a challenge that requires a lot of attention to Facebook groups and being aware of scammers etc.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I must say that I did find it a bit hard to register in classes in the online system, but once I arrived at the university everything was easier, and I got a lot of help from the staff at the exchange office at UVIC.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: There were online seminars hosted that told you about the different things you needed to in the semester before arriving. There was an access link that was sent to you sometime during mid-june to late-june, and this gave you access to the online sign up for classes. Here you had to look up classes and sign up for them - this was a bit confusing for me, because I couldn't find all the classes that I wanted, but also didn't just want to sign up for whatever. (But apparently you can sign up for a bunch and then you can drop the classes even after the semester abroad has started). I was nervous about this whole thing all summer, but it all turned out okay once I was at UVIC and the same goes for every other exchange student I knew at UVIC.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: In the time before arrival you were able to email the office at UVIC, but this wasn't very helpful to me because of the 9 hour time difference. What was most helpful was actually arriving in Victoria and visiting the exchange office in the week before classes officially started.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I didn't register for the classes that I initially wanted, but upon arrival I was able to enroll in classes that fulfilled the requirements I had for classes at UCPH.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The exchange office at UVIC is very helpful and if I was to redo it, I would maybe ask them if they would be available to do a teams-call with me, instead of emailing back and forth. Otherwise, try your best in the online system (UVIC will send information about how it works) and then if all else fails, just wait until you arrive and they will help you.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had 4 very good courses with engaged professors and teachers, and then I had 1 course that was essentially boring, because it was just lectures (and the lecturer read directly from the slides, very unenthusiastic) and there were no seminars, which meant that none of the students interacted with each other.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: All of my courses were 2nd-year level courses (and this you can tell by the number at the beginning of the course number, eg 220, 281)

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Class 1: lectures with a professor (200 students) + seminars with a teachers assistant (30 students)
Class 2: lectures with a professor (200 students)
Class 3: seminars with a professor (20 students)
Class 4: seminars with a professor (50 students)
Class 5: seminars with an Indigenous knowledge keeper (6 students)

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
COM220 Organizational Behavior
SOCI281 Sociology of Gender
ED-D219 Introduction to Indigenous Approaches to Helping and Healing
ED-D203 Leadership Theory and Practice 
PSYC201 Research Methods in Psychology

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I recommend any courses on Indigenous teachings and history (these can be found in a variety of faculties). These classes are incredibly unique, as they aren't taught globally, and the land on which the University of Victoria stands is connected deeply to Indigenous history and present time. There is a First Nations House in which most of these classes are taught, and it is one of the most beautiful places on campus. The teachers and professors that are teaching these classes are knowledgeable, kind and engaged, and I can't recommend it enough!

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: My rent was 880CAD, but every month there was a wifi+hydro+gas bill added, which was unpredictable. I also paid for membership in clubs at UVIC (climbing, kayaking, surfing, spinning etc.), as well as trips to other places in Canada, such as ski, camping and surf trips (which I couldn't budget for before, because I didn't know what trips I would go on).

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries were way more expensive than I had accounted for. And the books and bus-pass were more expensive as well, but I was able to find used books/online versions and I had access to a bike (which meant I didn't want to buy the semester bus-pass, but paid pr bus ride).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The clubs at UVIC are such a good opportunity to be social, go on trips and be active. I highly recommend joining the UVIC whitewater rafting kayak club, they did fun trips and social events. There was also a climbing club (with climbing once a week) that was fun. There was a surf club that did trips, but the sign up for these was hard and they sort of expected you to be a little better than just a beginner (but it was fun to go on the trip anyways). There is also a ski club, but it only does trips in the spring semester. There was a bunch of intramural teams (football, volleyball, basketball, ultimate frisbee, handball) that are fun to join. There is also the university gym (CARSA) that has good training facilities, and offers team training sessions such as spinning (really fun!).

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I recommend going to Tofino to camp with friends and surf or kayak, as well as do some hikes. I also recommend going to Strathcona Nationalpark, especially in late-spring to early-fall. I also recommend going to the Islands around Victoria, such as Hornby, Denman, Saltspring. It is pretty easy as well to do weekend trips to Seattle and Vancouver, which are accessible by ferry. There are also day trips from Victoria, such as Goldstream Provincial Park, Sooke Potholes and East Sooke Regional Park, and then the Juan De Fuca Coastline is amazing, with beaches such as China Beach, Botanical Beach, Sombrio, and Mystic Beach.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was fairly easy, because there was no language barrier. My roommates were good at explaining things and answering any questions I had, and the Canadians are super nice!

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I would join clubs at UVIC, they are usually run by local students, and they are very social students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I would say the only challenging thing to me, was that the students were generally very young, because they start university at an earlier age than Danish students usually do. This meant that I could have classes with 17 year-olds.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Canadians are nice and genuinely show interest in you, if you show interest in them. Bus drivers are kind and let everyone on the bus, all the staff at the university wanted to help you always, baristas at coffee shops talked to you about your day. If you meet someone you would love to get to know better, invite them for a coffee, a walk, a cold dip and they will most likely say yes! I have met some wonderful Canadian friends this way:)

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: The exchange office will help you, they are super nice! Sign up for clubs and extracurricular activities (especially if you don't live with canadian roommates)! And lastly, try your best to find off-campus housing with roommates, this will help you socially <3

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: most clubs "operate" on instagram, it can be a good idea to already look through UVIC's instagram to find clubs that you are interested in and keep up with their activities.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting wonderful people, genuine people that are my good friends now, and experiencing the beautiful nature in Canada. Victoria and Vancouver Island are exceptional!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: the biggest challenge was actually before, because I couldn't get my classes to workout, I was very very very nervous about this all summer. But everything worked out in the end, especially once I arrived in Victoria and could ask the exchange office for help.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: In Victoria you need two pieces of ID when you are buying alcoholic beverages in a bar/store/restaurant. This has to be one picture ID (passport, drivers license) and the second piece just needs your name (credit card, UVIC student card). The legal drinking age is 19.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
